title: Angles and creatives
summary: How to find problem-aware angles that stay honest, research them from real buyer language, write hooks, choose formats, localise for each geo and work with UGC creators within the rules. You finish with a testing structure that judges every creative on cost per approved lead.

lessons.title: Problem-aware angles that stay honest
objectives: By the end you can explain the difference between an angle, a hook and a format.
By the end you can write problem-aware angles that do not shame, diagnose or overpromise.
By the end you can build an angle list of at least six honest angles for one product.

steps.h: The angle is why someone stops
steps.p: An angle is the reason a person cares about your product. It decides who stops scrolling, what they expect and whether the call centre hears a happy buyer or a confused one. In nutra the angle also decides whether your ad is legal. Choose angles you can stand behind at the door.

d.s: Choose ones that stay true at delivery

steps.say: An angle is the reason a person cares about your product. It decides who stops scrolling, what they expect, and whether the call centre hears a happy buyer or a confused one. In nutra, the angle also decides whether your ad is legal. So choose angles that stay true at delivery, the kind you can stand behind when the parcel arrives at the door.

steps.p: Three words people mix up. The angle is the idea. The hook is the first line or first seconds that carry it. The format is the type of creative. One angle can have many hooks and formats, and you test them in that order.
d: Angle|the reason to care: long days on your feet
Hook|first 3 seconds: 'After 10 hours standing...'
Format|UGC, demo, static, carousel
Offer line|pay on delivery, price, delivery time
steps.say: Three words people mix up, shown on the cards. The angle is the idea, the reason to care, like long days on your feet. The hook is the first line or first three seconds that carry it, like after ten hours standing. The format is the type of creative: U G C, user-generated content, a demo, a static, or a carousel. And the offer line is pay on delivery, price and delivery time. One angle can have many hooks and formats, and you test them in that order.

steps.p: People meet your ad at different stages. Most nutra buyers are problem-aware: they know something bothers them but do not know your product. Your angle meets them there, without telling them what is wrong with them.

rows: A common situation, not a diagnosis

steps.say: People meet your ad at different stages, called awareness levels. Look at the table. Unaware people think nothing yet. Problem-aware people think, my knees feel tired. Solution-aware people think creams might help. Product-aware people have seen this cream. And the most aware just want it. Most nutra buyers are problem-aware. Your angle meets them there with a common situation, not a diagnosis, and without telling them what's wrong with them.

steps.p: You can name a common situation without telling the viewer they have a condition, without shaming and without promising a fix. Talk about situations and the product, not the viewer's body or illness.

b.title: Stays honest
items: A light cream for your evening routine
What is in the cream, line by line

steps.say: Here's how to be problem-aware without crossing the line. Compare the columns. On the left, lines that cross it: your knees are failing you, embarrassed by your skin, end joint pain for good, doctors are hiding this. On the right, lines that stay honest: after a long day standing, a light cream for your evening routine, a cooling feel after work, what's in the cream line by line. Talk about situations and the product, not the viewer's body or illness.

steps.p: Most honest nutra angles come from a few families. Each one leans on something true about the product or how it is bought. Build at least one angle from each family that fits your product before testing.
d: Situation|long shifts, hot weather, gym days
Ingredient|what is in it and why it is used
Routine|how it fits into a day
Convenience|pay on delivery, fast delivery
Value|price per day, bundle honestly priced
Real voices|real buyers, disclosed
steps.say: Most honest nutra angles come from a few families, on the cards. Situation, like long shifts, hot weather or gym days. Ingredient, what's in it and why. Routine, how it fits into a day. Convenience, pay on delivery and fast delivery. Value, price per day, or an honestly priced bundle. And real voices, real buyers, disclosed. Each leans on something true about the product or how it's bought. Build at least one angle from each family that fits before testing.

steps.p: Example: the 'long shifts' situation angle for a cooling joint cream in Nigeria. The ad never says the viewer has a condition. It describes a day many people recognise and shows what the product is.

messages.text: Hook A: Ten hours on your feet at the shop? This is how traders in Balogun end the day.
Hook B: The cooling cream nurses keep in their bag. Menthol, arnica, pay on delivery.
Hook C: 30 seconds after work: rub, cool, rest. Not a medicine, just a cooling cream.

steps.say: Here's one angle written three ways. Example: the long shifts angle, for a cooling joint cream in Nigeria. Hook A asks about ten hours on your feet at the shop, and shows how traders in Balogun end the day. Hook B says nurses keep this cooling cream in their bag. Hook C shows thirty seconds after work, and says plainly, not a medicine, just a cooling cream. Notice the ad never says the viewer has a condition.

steps.p: Hook B says nurses keep it in their bag. That is a claim about real people. Only use it if you can show it is true, for example with real, consenting nurses who bought it. Otherwise rewrite it.

d.text: Every specific claim in an angle, such as who uses it or how many bought it, must be true and provable. No invented groups, numbers or experts.

steps.say: Now look again at Hook B. It says nurses keep it in their bag. That's a claim about real people. Only use it if you can show it's true, for example with real, consenting nurses who bought it. Otherwise, rewrite it. The warning on screen applies to every angle: every specific claim, like who uses it or how many bought it, must be true and provable. No invented groups, numbers or experts.

steps.p: Example results after 4 days for three angles at the same budget. The convenience angle has the cheapest leads, but the routine angle has the best cost per approved lead, because buyers knew exactly what they ordered.
steps.more: Example: Routine $60 ÷ 6 = $10, under the $12 scale line (0.8 × the $15 target) with 6 approved, so it meets the scale rule. 'Pay on delivery' $60 ÷ 4 = $15 sits at target: keep it, do not scale it. 'Long shifts' is yours to call in the lab on the next slide. Starting rules; adapt to your offer, geo and data.
steps.say: Here are example results after four days for three angles, each spending sixty dollars. Long shifts got twelve leads and five approved, twelve dollars per approved lead. Routine got ten leads and six approved, ten dollars. Pay on delivery got the most leads, sixteen, but only four approved, fifteen dollars. So convenience has the cheapest leads, but routine has the best cost per approved lead, because buyers knew exactly what they ordered.

steps.p: Check the call for the first angle in the table with the calculator. Work out cost per approved lead, then compare it with the scale line and count the approved leads.
steps.more: Example: $60 ÷ 5 = $12, exactly the 0.8 × $15 scale line, with 5 approved. Scale +20%, then wait at least 48 hours before the next step.

d.task: Target $15. 'Long shifts' spent $60 in 4 days, 5 approved leads. Kill, hold or scale?

steps.say: Lab time. Take the first angle in the table, long shifts. The target is fifteen dollars. It spent sixty dollars over four days, with five approved leads. Use the calculator to work out the cost per approved lead, then compare it with the scale line, and count the approved leads. Then make the call: kill, hold or scale. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.p: These are the angle mistakes that waste test budgets in nutra. Most come from copying what looks loud in a rival's feed instead of building from what is true about your product and buyer.

b.title: Fixes
items: Judge on cost per approved lead

steps.say: These are the angle mistakes that waste test budgets in nutra. Compare the columns. One angle with ten hooks, when you should test three or more angles first. An angle built on a fear, instead of a real situation. Judging angles on C P L, cost per lead, instead of cost per approved lead. And copying a rival's claim, instead of building from your claims file. Most come from copying what looks loud in a rival's feed.

steps.p: Use this sequence for every new product. It takes an hour and gives you a list of angles that are legal, varied and ready for hooks. Keep the list in the same folder as the claims file.
d: Read the claims file
List real buyer situations
Write 1 angle per family
Remove any that need a claim you lack
Pick 3 to test first
steps.say: Here's how to build your angle list, in about an hour, for every new product. Follow the flow. Read the claims file. List real buyer situations. Write one angle per family. Remove any that need a claim you don't have. And pick three to test first. You end up with angles that are legal, varied and ready for hooks. Keep the list in the same folder as the claims file.

steps.p: A note from the founder on finding angles in a crowded, aggressive vertical, where many rival ads still lean on claims and tricks that this school does not teach.
steps.d: When everyone in the feed is shouting cures, the calm ad that tells the truth about a real day stands out. Quiet can be a strategy.
steps.say: Here's a note from Dchessking on finding angles in a crowded, aggressive vertical, where many rival ads still lean on claims and tricks this school doesn't teach. In his words: When everyone in the feed is shouting cures, the calm ad that tells the truth about a real day stands out. Quiet can be a strategy.

takeaways: Angle is the reason to care, hook carries it, format is the creative type.
Problem-aware angles describe common situations, never the viewer's condition, and never shame.
Test at least three angles and judge them on cost per approved lead.
lessons.action: For one nutra product, write six honest angles (one per family), cross out any that need a claim not in your claims file, and pick three to test.

The first line or first seconds of a creative that carry the angle.

quiz.q: Which is a hook, not an angle?
options: After 10 hours standing at the shop...
quiz.why: The hook is the opening line or seconds that carry an angle.

quiz.q: Which problem-aware line stays honest?
quiz.why: It describes a common situation without diagnosing, shaming or promising.

quiz.q: Angle A: $60, 5 approved. Angle B: $60, 4 approved. Target $15, scale line $12. Decision?
quiz.why: A: $12, meets scale with 5 approved. B: $15, at target, keep.

quiz.q: Your hook says nurses use the cream. When can you use it?
options: Only if it is true and provable
quiz.why: Claims about real groups of users must be true and provable.

quiz.q: Which order do you test in?
quiz.why: The angle has the biggest effect; hooks and formats are tested inside a winning angle.

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll learn how to choose nutra angles that make people stop and still stay honest. You'll separate angle, hook and format, and build a list of at least six angles you can stand behind.
lessons.say_outro: So, an angle is the reason to care, it should describe a real situation rather than a diagnosis, and you judge it on cost per approved lead. lessons.title: Researching angles the honest way
objectives: By the end you can collect angle ideas from ad libraries, comments, reviews and call centre feedback.
By the end you can tally buyer language into themes and turn them into angles.
By the end you can study rival ads without copying their claims or creatives.

steps.p: Every angle you test costs money. Angles taken from real buyer language usually find a winner with fewer tests than angles you invent at your desk. Research is cheap: a few hours of reading saves a few hundred dollars of tests.
steps.say: Research beats guessing. Every angle you test costs money. Angles taken from real buyer language usually find a winner with fewer tests than angles you invent at your desk. And research is cheap. A few hours of reading can save a few hundred dollars of tests. So listen before you write. Buyers will tell you the angle.

steps.p: Use several sources, because each one is biased in a different way. Ad libraries show what advertisers try, not what works. Comments show real words. The call centre hears the objections that kill approval.
d: Ad libraries|what rivals are running now
Comments|buyers' own words and doubts
Product reviews|what people liked and missed
Call centre|top reasons people say no
Forums and groups|everyday language
Search trends|what people ask about
steps.say: Here's where to listen, on the cards. Ad libraries show what rivals are running now. Comments show buyers' own words and doubts. Product reviews show what people liked and missed. The call centre hears the top reasons people say no. Forums and groups show everyday language. And search trends show what people ask about. Use several sources, because each one is biased differently. For example, ad libraries show what advertisers try, not what works.

steps.h: Studying rival ads in an ad library

steps.title: Search
steps.text: Choose the country and 'All ads', then search a product type, not a brand.

steps.title: Note long runners
steps.text: Ads running for weeks are more likely to be working. Note the start date.

steps.title: Record the idea
steps.text: Write down the angle and format, never the claims or the creative itself.

steps.say: Let's walk through studying rival ads in a public ad library. Meta's Ad Library lists ads currently running, by country. Tap Next to follow each step. First, search: choose the country and all ads, then search a product type, like joint cream, not a brand. Second, note the long runners, because ads running for weeks are more likely to be working, so note the start date. Third, record the idea, the angle and format, never the claims or the creative itself. Layouts change, so check the current version.

steps.p: Once you know what to look for, a spy tool saves time by showing many live ads by geo and vertical in one place. Use it for ideas and timing, never to copy creatives or claims.

d.why: Spyvoo shows live ads by geo and vertical, so you can see which angles and formats rivals keep running before you plan your own tests.

steps.p: Rival ads in nutra often contain banned claims, fake doctors and stolen footage. Copying them copies their legal risk and may infringe their copyright. Take the idea of an angle, then build it from your own claims file and your own footage.

d.text: Never copy a rival's creative, footage or claims. Long-running ads can still be non-compliant; check every idea against your claims file.

steps.say: Research isn't copying. Rival ads in nutra often contain banned claims, fake doctors and stolen footage. Copying them copies their legal risk, and may infringe their copyright. Take the idea of an angle, then build it from your own claims file and your own footage. The warning on screen adds an important point: long-running ads can still be non-compliant, so check every idea against your claims file.

steps.p: Example: you read 60 comments under nutra ads for joint creams in your geo and tag each with a theme. The biggest themes become your first angles. Doubts are as useful as praise: they tell you what to answer.
steps.more: Example: 18 + 14 + 12 + 8 + 8 = 60 comments. The bar length is each count compared with the largest (18). 'Is it real or fake?' at 14 suggests a trust angle: show the real product, the real ingredients and pay on delivery so people can check before paying.
d: Long working days
Is it real or fake?
Price and delivery
Smell and feel
Age and stairs
steps.say: Here's how to tally comments into themes. Example: you read sixty comments under joint cream ads in your geo, and tag each one. Look at the bars. Long working days, eighteen. Is it real or fake, fourteen. Price and delivery, twelve. Smell and feel, eight. Age and stairs, eight. The biggest themes become your first angles. And doubts are as useful as praise. Is it real or fake suggests a trust angle: show the real product, real ingredients, and pay on delivery.

steps.p: Your network can often share why leads were rejected. Those reasons are angle research. If many people say 'I thought it was a medicine', your ad is promising too much. Ask for the top reasons every week.

messages.text: Can you share the top rejection reasons for my leads this week?
Top three: price too high, thought it was free, did not remember ordering.
Thanks. I will show the price on the lander and add a clear order step.

steps.say: Ask the call centre, through your network. They can often share why leads were rejected, and those reasons are angle research. In this example chat, the top three are price too high, thought it was free, and didn't remember ordering. So the buyer plans to show the price on the lander and add a clear order step. If many people say, I thought it was a medicine, your ad is promising too much. Ask for the top reasons every week.

steps.p: Turn each theme into an angle you can prove, and note what each one needs. If you cannot prove it, drop it, however popular the theme is.
steps.say: Now turn research into angles. Look at the table. Long working days becomes an end-of-shift routine, which needs nothing beyond product facts. Is it real becomes show the real product, which needs real footage and the real price. Price and delivery becomes pay when it arrives, with correct prices and delivery times. Age and stairs becomes a light routine for active days, with no mobility claims unless proven. If you can't prove it, drop it, however popular the theme is.

steps.p: These research mistakes lead to angles that are either illegal or untested guesses dressed up as research. Most come from using one source only, or from reading only in English when buyers speak other languages.
d: Copying long runners|they can still be illegal
Only reading praise|doubts show what to answer
Ignoring the call centre|it hears why people say no
English-only research|buyers speak other languages
No record|you repeat failed angles
steps.say: These research mistakes lead to angles that are either illegal, or guesses dressed up as research. Copying long runners, which can still be illegal. Only reading praise, when doubts show what to answer. Ignoring the call centre, which hears why people say no. English-only research, when buyers speak other languages. And keeping no record, so you repeat failed angles.

steps.p: Keep research steady rather than one big burst before a launch. Thirty minutes a week, on the same day, keeps your angle bank full and current, and shows you when buyer language starts to change.
d: Check ad library for your product type and geo
Read 20 new comments, tag themes
Ask the network for rejection reasons
Add 2 new angles to the bank
Retire angles that failed twice
steps.say: Keep research steady with this weekly routine, about thirty minutes on the same day. Check the ad library for your product type and geo. Read twenty new comments and tag themes. Ask the network for rejection reasons. Add two new angles to the bank. And retire angles that failed twice. It keeps your angle bank full and current, and shows you when buyer language starts to change.

takeaways: Use ad libraries, comments, reviews and call centre reasons; each shows something different.
Tally buyer language into themes; the largest themes and the strongest doubts become angles.
Take ideas, never creatives or claims, from rival ads.

lessons.title: Hooks and formats that work for nutra
objectives: By the end you can write and storyboard the first three seconds of a nutra video.
By the end you can choose a format for each angle and explain why.
By the end you can read hook rate and CTR to decide which hooks to keep.

steps.p: On Meta and TikTok, most people scroll past in the first seconds. A hook that stops more people lowers your cost per click and per lead. In nutra, the hook must stop people with something true, not with shock or shame.
steps.say: Three seconds decide the cost. On Meta and TikTok, most people scroll past in the first seconds. A hook that stops more people lowers your cost per click, and per lead. But in nutra, the hook must stop people with something true, not with shock or shame. Stop the scroll honestly.

steps.p: Each format suits different angles. Test at least two formats inside a winning angle. Keep all of them inside the visual rules from the compliance module.
d: UGC talking|a real buyer explains their routine
Texture demo|close-up of the product in use
Ingredient explainer|what is in it, one line each
Day in the life|where it fits in a routine
Static with price|product, price, pay on delivery
FAQ carousel|answers doubts one card at a time
steps.say: Here are the formats for nutra, on the cards. U G C talking, user-generated content, where a real buyer explains their routine. A texture demo, a close-up of the product in use. An ingredient explainer, one line each. Day in the life, where it fits in a routine. A static with price, product and pay on delivery. And an F A Q carousel, answering doubts one card at a time. Test at least two formats inside a winning angle, all within the compliance module's visual rules.

steps.p: These patterns stop people without shaming, diagnosing or overpromising. Fill them with your angle and the product facts from your claims file, then write three to five versions of each before choosing which to film.

rows: Ten hours at the shop today?
This is what the cream looks like up close
What is actually in a cooling cream?
I asked five traders what they use after work
It is not a medicine. Here is what it is.

steps.say: These hook patterns stop people without shaming, diagnosing or overpromising. Situation: ten hours at the shop today? Show the product: this is what the cream looks like up close. A question about the product: what's actually in a cooling cream? Real voice: I asked five traders what they use after work. And honest contrast: it's not a medicine, here's what it is. Fill them with your angle and claims file facts, and write three to five versions of each.

steps.say: Let's storyboard a twenty-second U G C ad for the end-of-shift routine angle. Tap Next to follow each shot. Zero to three seconds, the hook: a trader packing up her stall, with the text, ten hours standing today. Three to ten seconds, the product: she shows the texture and rubs it on her knees. Ten to sixteen seconds, the honest line: it feels cool, I like it, it's not a medicine, with a disclosure that she got a free tube. Sixteen to twenty seconds, the offer: price, pay on delivery, delivery time.

steps.p: Hook rate is not a standard platform metric, so teams compute it themselves: 3-second video plays divided by impressions. It tells you whether the opening stops people. Metric names change; check what your Ads Manager reports.
steps.more: Example: 3,000 three-second plays from 10,000 impressions is 30%. A hook at 30% and another at 15% on the same angle and audience tell you which opening to keep. Rough guide only: what counts as good varies by geo, placement and format.

steps.say: Hook rate isn't a standard platform metric, so teams work it out themselves. Follow the formula: three-second video plays, divided by impressions. It tells you whether the opening stops people. For example, three thousand plays from ten thousand impressions is thirty percent. What counts as good varies by geo, placement and format. Metric names change too, so check what your Ads Manager reports.

steps.p: Example after two days, same angle, same audience. Hook C stops the most people but its leads are poorly approved, because a dramatic first line sets the wrong expectation. Judge the whole chain, not the hook alone.
steps.more: Example: with a $15 target and $20 kill line, C is above target and close to the kill line despite the best hook rate and CTR. If it reaches 3 × target spend ($45) above $20 per approved lead, kill it. B is the strongest on money even though it stops fewer people.

blocks.value: Example. Per approved = spend ÷ network-approved leads for each ad's sub-ID.

steps.p: Hook tests need many versions of the same ad with different openings. A creative tool can speed up making those versions from your own footage and approved claims. Check every output against your claims file before use.

steps.p: These are the hook mistakes that cost nutra buyers the most money. Several of them also break platform policy, so they cost twice: once in poor approval and again in rejected ads.

Keeping the hook with best CTR only

b.title: Fixes

Price and pay on delivery on screen

steps.say: These hook mistakes cost nutra buyers the most money, and several break platform policy, so they cost twice. Compare the columns. Shock or shame in the opening, instead of a true situation. Keeping only the hook with the best C T R, instead of judging on cost per approved lead. Never showing the product, instead of showing the real product early. And no price or delivery info, instead of price and pay on delivery on screen.

steps.p: Use this checklist each time you test new hooks. Changing only the opening keeps the test clean, so you know the hook caused the difference.
d: Same angle, body and offer line
Only the first 3 seconds change
3 to 5 hooks per test
Each hook in its own ad with its own tracking ID
Judge after the leads are processed
steps.say: Use this checklist each time you test new hooks. Keep the same angle, body and offer line. Change only the first three seconds. Test three to five hooks. Put each hook in its own ad, with its own tracking I D. And judge only after the leads are processed. Changing only the opening keeps the test clean, so you know the hook caused the difference.

takeaways: The first three seconds set your cost; stop people with something true.
Choose formats per angle: UGC, demo, ingredient explainer, routine, static, FAQ carousel.
Hook rate and CTR are signals; keep the hook with the best cost per approved lead.

options: Ten hours at the shop today?
quiz.why: It names a common situation without shaming or promising.

quiz.q: You use AI to make a realistic 'customer' praising the cream. What is the problem?
options: It invents a customer, which is a fake testimonial
quiz.why: AI-made customers are fake endorsements and deceptive.

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll learn to write honest hooks and pick the right format for each angle. You'll storyboard the first seconds of a nutra video, and use hook rate and C T R to decide which hooks to keep.
lessons.say_outro: So, the first three seconds decide the cost, the hook must be true, and you keep hooks by cost per approved lead, not by hook rate alone. Your task: write five honest hooks for your best angle using this lesson's patterns, and storyboard one twenty-second video with hook, product, honest line and offer. Now take the quiz.

lessons.title: Localising nutra creatives by geo
objectives: By the end you can list what must change in a creative when you move to a new geo.
By the end you can brief a native speaker to localise copy and voice.
By the end you can compare localised and non-localised results on cost per approved lead.

steps.p: A translated ad says the same words in another language. A localised ad feels like it was made for the buyer: their language or mix of languages, their money, their cities, their daily life. Localised ads usually earn more trust, better approval and fewer refused parcels.
steps.say: Translation isn't localisation. A translated ad says the same words in another language. A localised ad feels like it was made for the buyer: their language or mix of languages, their money, their cities, their daily life. Localised ads usually earn more trust, better approval, and fewer refused parcels. Make it feel local.

steps.p: Check every item when you move a creative to a new country. Missing one, such as the currency or a delivery city, makes the ad feel foreign and lowers trust at the call.
d: Language|including mixes like Pidgin or Sheng
Money|local currency and real price
Places|cities you actually deliver to
People and settings|who and where buyers recognise
Payment line|pay on delivery, mobile money if offered
Law|claims and disclaimers allowed there
steps.say: Check every item on these cards when you move a creative to a new country. Language, including mixes like Pidgin or Sheng. Money, the local currency and real price. Places, cities you actually deliver to. People and settings buyers recognise. The payment line, pay on delivery, or mobile money if offered. And law, the claims and disclaimers allowed there. Missing just one, like the currency or a delivery city, makes the ad feel foreign and lowers trust at the call.

steps.p: Examples of language choices in common COD geos. Rough guide only; ask native speakers which mix your buyers actually use, and match the call centre's language.
steps.say: Here are example language choices in common C O D, cash on delivery, geos. Nigeria: English, Pidgin, Yoruba, Hausa and Igbo, with Pidgin reaching widely. Kenya: English, Swahili and Sheng, which is mostly urban and younger. Ghana: English and Twi. Cameroon: French and English, matching the region. Côte d'Ivoire: French, with local expressions. And the Philippines: Filipino, English and Taglish. It's a rough guide, so ask native speakers which mix your buyers use, and match the call centre's language.

steps.p: Example: the same cooling cream ad for Kenya. The left version is a straight translation from a Nigerian ad. The right version is localised by a Kenyan speaker with real delivery details.

b.title: Localised
items: Price in KES, as on the lander

steps.say: Here's the same cooling cream ad for Kenya, two ways. Compare the columns. The translated version, copied from a Nigerian ad, shows the price in U S dollars, says delivery in major cities, uses Lagos market footage, and formal Swahili. The localised version, made by a Kenyan speaker, shows the price in Kenyan shillings as on the lander, names Nairobi, Mombasa and Kisumu, uses footage from a Nairobi market, and everyday Swahili and English.

steps.p: Example: the lander matches the ad's language and money, names real delivery cities and says plainly what the product is. The call centre for this offer must speak Swahili and English.

page.p: Cooling cream with menthol. Lipa ukipokea: Nairobi, Mombasa, Kisumu. Si dawa; matokeo hutofautiana.

steps.say: Here's a localised lander for Kenya. It matches the ad's language and money, names real delivery cities, pay on delivery in Nairobi, Mombasa and Kisumu, and says plainly in Swahili that it's not a medicine, and results vary. It describes the product simply, a cooling cream with menthol. And for this offer, the call centre must speak both Swahili and English, so the conversation matches the page.

steps.p: Example from two ad sets with the same budget and audience. The localised version has slightly more expensive leads but much better approval, so it wins on cost per approved lead.
steps.more: Example: $5.00 ÷ 0.35 = $14.29. $5.50 ÷ 0.55 = $10.00. With a $15 target, the translated version is just under target and the localised version is under the $12 scale line. The better approval comes from buyers who understood exactly what they ordered.

blocks.value: Example. Approval from the network after processing.

steps.say: Here's an example test from two ad sets, same budget, same audience. The translated version has a five dollar C P L, cost per lead, thirty five percent approval, and fourteen twenty nine per approved lead. The localised version has a five fifty C P L, but fifty five percent approval, so ten dollars per approved lead. Its leads are slightly more expensive, but it wins on cost per approved lead, because buyers understood exactly what they ordered.

steps.p: Hire a native speaker who lives in the geo, not only a translator. Give them a clear brief so they keep the meaning and the compliance limits while making the copy sound natural.
d: Share the angle and the claims file
List words and claims that must not appear
Ask for everyday language, not formal
Ask them to check prices and cities
Have them review the voice-over too
Pay fairly and agree usage in writing
steps.say: Hire a native speaker who lives in the geo, not only a translator, and give them a clear brief. Follow the checklist. Share the angle and the claims file. List the words and claims that must not appear. Ask for everyday language, not formal. Ask them to check prices and cities. Have them review the voice-over too. And pay fairly, with usage agreed in writing. That way they keep the meaning and the compliance limits, while making the copy sound natural.

steps.p: A safe English sentence can become a stronger claim in translation, for example when 'soothing' is translated as a word that means 'heals'. Ask the speaker to translate the final copy back into English so you can check the meaning.

d.text: Back-translate every localised ad and lander into English and check it against your claims file. Disclaimers must be in the buyer's language.

steps.say: Compliance changes with the language. A safe English sentence can become a stronger claim in translation. For example, soothing might be translated as a word that means heals. So ask the speaker to translate the final copy back into English, so you can check the meaning. The warning on screen: back-translate every localised ad and lander into English, check it against your claims file, and make sure disclaimers are in the buyer's language.

steps.p: These mistakes show up most when a team copies a winning ad into a new geo in a hurry. Each one lowers trust or creates a claim problem.
d: Machine translation only|meaning and tone drift
Wrong currency or price|refusals at the door
Cities you do not serve|rejected on the call
Disclaimer left in English|buyer cannot read it
Footage from another country|feels foreign
steps.say: These mistakes show up most when a team copies a winning ad into a new geo in a hurry. Machine translation only, where meaning and tone drift. The wrong currency or price, which means refusals at the door. Cities you don't serve, so leads are rejected on the call. A disclaimer left in English that the buyer can't read. And footage from another country that feels foreign.

steps.h: Moving a winner to a new geo
steps.p: Use this order when a creative wins in one country and you want to try it in another. It keeps the angle, which is often what won, and rebuilds everything that is local.
d: Keep the winning angle
Check law and claims for the new geo
Localise copy with a native speaker
Reshoot or source local footage
Back-translate and review
Test against a fresh local angle
steps.say: Here's the order to follow when a creative wins in one country and you want to try it in another. Keep the winning angle, because that's often what won. Check law and claims for the new geo. Localise the copy with a native speaker. Reshoot, or source local footage. Back-translate and review. And test it against a fresh local angle. You keep what won, and rebuild everything that's local.

takeaways: Localise language, money, places, people and payment lines, not just words.
Brief native speakers with the claims file and back-translate to check meaning.
Judge localised versions on cost per approved lead; approval often moves most.
lessons.action: Take one winning or planned ad and list every element that would change for a second geo. Write a brief for a native speaker using the checklist from this lesson.

glossary.def: Adapting a creative so it feels made for buyers in a specific place, beyond translation.
Translating localised copy back into the original language to check its meaning.
Nigerian Pidgin, an English-based language widely spoken in Nigeria.
A Swahili and English based slang used mostly in urban Kenya.

quiz.q: CPL $5.50, approval 55%. Cost per approved lead?
Why back-translate a localised ad?
options: To check the meaning has not become a stronger claim
quiz.why: Translation can turn safe words into medical claims.

quiz.q: Your Kenyan lander names Lagos delivery. What is the likely result?
options: Confused buyers and rejected leads on the call
quiz.why: Wrong places make the offer feel foreign and fail at confirmation.

quiz.q: Which is localisation, not just translation?
options: Using local currency, cities, language mix and settings
quiz.why: Localisation adapts everything the buyer sees.

quiz.q: Where should the disclaimer be in a French-speaking geo?
quiz.why: The buyer must be able to read and understand it.

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll learn why translation isn't localisation, what must change when you move a nutra creative to a new country, and how to brief a native speaker so the ad feels local and stays compliant.
lessons.say_outro: So, localising means language, money, places and daily life, checked by a native speaker and back-translated against your claims file. Your task: take one winning or planned ad, list every element that would change for a second geo, and write a brief for a native speaker using this lesson's checklist. Now take the quiz.

lessons.title: UGC and creators: rules and briefs
objectives: By the end you can source real creators and write a compliant UGC brief.
By the end you can agree usage rights, disclosure and payment in writing.
By the end you can review a UGC video against claims and platform rules.

steps.h: UGC works because it feels real
steps.p: User-generated content works in nutra because it looks like a real person talking. That is also why it is risky: if the person is not a real user, or says things that are not true, the ad deceives buyers. The rules protect both the buyer and your account.

d.b: Real people, real use, real words

steps.say: U G C, user-generated content, works in nutra because it looks like a real person talking. That's also why it's risky. If the person isn't a real user, or says things that aren't true, the ad deceives buyers. The rules protect both the buyer and your account. So remember the line on screen: real people, real use, real words, disclosed and agreed in writing.

steps.p: There are honest ways to get UGC. Each needs consent, disclosure and a check of what they say. Actors can show a product but must not pretend to be customers with results.
d: Real buyers|best, with consent and disclosure
Creators who try it|send product, ask for honest use
Actors|may demonstrate, not claim results
Your team|disclose who they are
AI avatars|not as customers or experts
steps.say: There are honest ways to get U G C, shown on the cards. Real buyers are best, with consent and disclosure. Creators who try it, where you send the product and ask for honest use. Actors, who may demonstrate, but must not claim results or pretend to be customers. Your team, as long as you disclose who they are. And A I avatars, never as customers or experts. Each needs consent, disclosure, and a check of what they say.

steps.p: A good brief makes compliant content the easy path for the creator. Send it before they film, and ask them to confirm they have read the banned list.
d: Angle and situation to show
Product facts they may mention
Banned words: cure, treat, heal, disease names
No before-and-after, no body shaming
Disclosure line to say or show
Length, format, language and deadline
steps.say: A good brief makes compliant content the easy path for the creator. Here's what it includes. The angle and situation to show. The product facts they may mention. The banned words: cure, treat, heal, and disease names. No before-and-after, and no body shaming. The disclosure line to say or show. And the length, format, language and deadline. Send it before they film, and ask them to confirm they've read the banned list.

steps.p: Example of sending a brief to a creator in Ghana. It is short, clear on what not to say and asks for their honest experience rather than a script of claims.

messages.text: Hi Kofi, brief attached. Please use the cream for a week and film a 20 s video about your evening routine.
Say only what you notice, like the feel or smell. Please do not mention any illness or say it heals anything.
OK. Do I say you sent it?
Yes, please say 'They sent me this to try' and we will add a paid partnership label too.

steps.say: Here's an example of sending a brief to Kofi, a creator in Ghana. It asks him to use the cream for a week and film a twenty-second video about his evening routine. It says to mention only what he notices, like feel or smell, and not to mention any illness or say it heals anything. When he asks whether to say they sent it, the answer is yes, say they sent me this to try, and a paid partnership label is added too.

steps.p: Agree these terms before filming. Without written rights, a creator can ask you to remove a winning ad, or you can end up running content you are not allowed to use.

rows: Cuts and captions, no new claims

steps.say: Agree usage rights in writing before filming. Here's an example. Where it runs: Meta and TikTok ads. Geos: Ghana and Nigeria. How long: six months, renewable. Edits allowed: cuts and captions, but no new claims. Payment: sixty dollars per video plus product. And disclosure: spoken and on screen. Without written rights, a creator can ask you to remove a winning ad, or you can end up running content you're not allowed to use.

steps.p: Example: plan for some videos not being usable, because they include banned claims, poor sound or the wrong angle. Budget for the usable ones, not the number of creators you hire, and agree re-shoots in advance.
steps.more: Example only. 8 × $68 = $544. If 5 videos pass review, each usable video cost $544 ÷ 5 = $108.80. Ask for re-shoots in the agreement so a video with one banned line can be fixed rather than wasted.
d: 8 creators × ($60 + $8)
÷ 5 usable
steps.say: Plan for some videos not being usable, because of banned claims, poor sound, or the wrong angle. Follow the example. Eight creators at sixty dollars plus eight dollars of product is five hundred and forty four dollars. If five videos pass review, each usable video cost about one hundred and eight dollars eighty. So budget for usable videos, not the number of creators, and agree re-shoots in advance so one banned line can be fixed rather than wasted.

steps.p: Paid or gifted content must be disclosed. Meta and TikTok have their own branded content tools and labels, such as a paid partnership label, and their names and rules change. We are not certain this is current; check the platform's Help Center before relying on it.

d.text: Disclose payment or free product clearly in the video and use the platform's branded content tools where required. We are not certain this is current; check the platform's Help Center before relying on it.

steps.say: Paid or gifted content must be disclosed. Meta and TikTok have their own branded content tools and labels, like a paid partnership label, and their names and rules change. The warning on screen: disclose payment or free product clearly in the video, and use the platform's branded content tools where required. We're not certain this is current, so check the platform's Help Center before relying on it.

steps.p: These mistakes turn UGC from a strength into a risk. Several are illegal under endorsement and consumer rules in many countries, and all of them can get ads rejected or accounts restricted.

a.title: Mistakes
items: Actor posing as a buyer with results

steps.say: These mistakes turn U G C from a strength into a risk. Several are illegal under endorsement and consumer rules in many countries. Compare the columns. A script with cure claims, instead of a brief with banned words. An actor posing as a buyer with results, when actors should demonstrate only. No written usage rights, instead of agreeing rights before filming. And no disclosure, instead of spoken and on-screen disclosure.

steps.p: Example review of a delivered video. Watch it twice: once as a buyer, once with the checklist. Note timestamps of anything that needs a cut or re-shoot.

steps.title: Watch as a buyer
steps.text: What would a typical viewer believe after watching?

page.p: Kofi shows the cream after work.

steps.title: Check claims
steps.text: At 0:12 he says 'it healed my back'. Mark for cut or re-shoot.

steps.title: Approve or return
steps.text: Send notes. Approve only after fixes.

messages.text: Great video. Could you re-record 0:12 without 'healed'? Say how it feels instead.

steps.say: Let's walk through reviewing a delivered video. Watch it twice: once as a buyer, once with the checklist. Tap Next to follow each step. First, watch as a buyer, and ask what a typical viewer would believe. Second, check claims. At twelve seconds, Kofi says it healed my back, so that's marked for a cut or re-shoot, and at eighteen seconds there's no disclosure, so add it on screen. Third, send notes and approve only after fixes. Here, Kofi agrees to re-record the line describing how it feels instead.

steps.h: Keep on file for each video
steps.p: Store these with the claims file for each video. Together they prove the creator is real, agreed to the use, was told the rules and was paid as agreed, if a platform or network ever asks.
d: Signed agreement|rights, geos, duration
Brief sent|with banned list
Raw footage|before edits
Review notes|what was cut and why
Payment record|amount and date
steps.say: Keep these on file for each video, stored with the claims file. The signed agreement, with rights, geos and duration. The brief you sent, with the banned list. The raw footage, before edits. Your review notes, what was cut and why. And the payment record, amount and date. Together, they prove the creator is real, agreed to the use, was told the rules, and was paid as agreed, if a platform or network ever asks.

takeaways: UGC must come from real people describing real use, with disclosure and written consent.
Briefs list banned words and visuals; actors may demonstrate but not claim results.
Agree usage rights, edits and payment before filming, and review every video before use.
lessons.action: Write a one-page UGC brief for one product with angle, allowed facts, banned words, disclosure line and usage terms, and send it to one real creator or buyer.

glossary.def: What you may do with a creator's content: where, where geographically, for how long and with what edits.
Posts or ads made with a creator for a brand, which platforms require to be labelled.
A platform label showing content is paid or gifted. Names vary and change.
Filming a part again to fix a problem.

quiz.q: May an actor say 'this cream healed my knees' in your ad?
options: No, actors may demonstrate but not claim results, and healing is a disease claim
quiz.why: Actors posing as customers with results are deceptive, and healing is a disease claim.

quiz.q: 8 creators at $68 each, 5 usable. Cost per usable video?
What must a UGC brief include?
options: Banned words and the disclosure line
quiz.why: Briefs make compliant content the easy path.

quiz.q: A creator's video says 'healed' at 0:12. What do you do?
options: Cut or re-shoot that line before use
quiz.why: Remove the disease claim before the video runs.

quiz.q: Why agree usage rights before filming?
options: So the creator cannot be paid
So you can run the content where and as long as agreed
quiz.why: Without written rights you may lose or misuse the content.

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll learn how to get honest U G C, user-generated content, for nutra. You'll write a compliant brief, agree rights, disclosure and payment in writing, and review a delivered video before it runs.
lessons.say_outro: So, honest U G C means real people, a brief with banned words, written rights, clear disclosure, and a careful review before launch. Your task: write a one-page U G C brief for one product with angle, allowed facts, banned words, disclosure line and usage terms, and send it to one real creator or buyer. Now take the quiz.

lessons.title: Creative testing and fatigue for COD
objectives: By the end you can structure an angle and hook test with tracking per creative.
By the end you can apply kill, hold and scale rules to creatives using approved leads.
By the end you can spot creative fatigue and plan refreshes.

steps.h: Test creatives on money, not likes
steps.p: In COD nutra, a creative's job is to bring buyers who get approved and accept the parcel. Likes, CTR and cheap leads are signals. To judge a creative you need approvals per creative, which means a tracking ID on every ad.
steps.say: In C O D, cash on delivery, nutra, a creative's job is to bring buyers who get approved and accept the parcel. Likes, C T R, click-through rate, and cheap leads are only signals. To judge a creative, you need approvals per creative. And that means a tracking I D on every ad. Tag every ad.

steps.h: Pass the ad ID to the network
steps.p: Most networks accept sub-IDs on your link. Put the ad ID in one of them so each approved lead can be traced to a creative. Macro names differ by platform and tracker; check the current documentation.

d.note: Example with Meta-style URL parameters. Names change; check Ads Manager.

steps.say: Most networks accept sub I Ds on your link. Put the ad I D in one of them, so each approved lead can be traced back to a creative. The link on screen is an example using Meta-style U R L parameters. I won't read it out, but notice it carries the campaign, the ad set and the ad, plus a readable creative name. Macro names differ by platform and tracker and they change, so check the current documentation.

steps.p: Example: one campaign, one ad set per angle, three to five hooks per ad set. Each ad has its own sub-ID. This keeps the angle test clean and lets you read hooks inside each angle.
steps.say: Here's a simple test structure, as a map. One campaign, the Nigerian joint cream. One ad set per angle: long shifts, routine, and pay on delivery. Three to five hooks in each ad set. And each ad has its own sub I D, flowing into the network's sub I D report as approvals. This keeps the angle test clean, and lets you read hooks inside each angle.

steps.p: The same rule card as the rest of the school, applied per ad set and per creative with network-approved leads. Example: target $15, break-even $20. Starting rules; adapt to your offer, geo and data.

rows: Spend ≥ 3 × target, CPA over kill line

steps.say: Here's the creative rule card, the same as the rest of the school, applied per ad set and per creative, with network-approved leads. Example: target fifteen dollars, break-even twenty. Kill at thirty dollars spend with zero approved. Kill from forty five dollars if C P A, cost per approved lead, is over twenty. Scale by twenty percent with three or more approved and C P A at or under twelve, at least forty eight hours apart. Keep at twelve to fifteen. Anything else is a hold, wait for processing. Adapt these starting rules to your data.

steps.p: Apply the rule card to one ad set. All of its leads have been processed by the call centre, so the approved count is final enough to judge. Work out cost per approved lead first.
steps.more: Example: $54 ÷ 5 = $10.80, under the $12 scale line with 5 approved. Scale +20%, then wait at least 48 hours. Inside the ad set, move nothing; let the best hooks keep spending.

d.task: Target $15. Ad set 'Routine' spent $54 in 3 days, 5 approved leads. Kill, hold or scale?

steps.say: Lab time. Apply the rule card to one ad set. All its leads have been processed by the call centre, so the approved count is final enough to judge. The target is fifteen dollars. The routine ad set spent fifty four dollars over three days, with five approved leads. Work out the cost per approved lead first, then check it against each row of the card. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.p: One more. Leads are processed, but spend is still small compared with the target. Decide carefully: not every bad-looking number is a kill, and killing too early wastes the test.
steps.more: Example: $24 per approved lead is above the kill line, but spend is under 3 × $15 = $45, so the CPA kill rule does not apply yet, and it has 1 approved so the zero-approval rule does not apply. Hold, change nothing.

d.task: Target $15. Ad set 'Long shifts' spent $24 in 2 days, 1 approved lead. Kill, hold or scale?

steps.say: One more. This time, leads are processed, but spend is still small compared with the target. The long shifts ad set spent twenty four dollars over two days, with one approved lead. Decide carefully, because not every bad-looking number is a kill, and killing too early wastes the test. Check each rule's spend threshold as well as the C P A. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.p: Example: a winning creative over 7 days. Frequency climbs as the same people see it again, CTR falls and cost per approved lead rises. This is fatigue. Plan the refresh before the numbers cross your kill line.
steps.more: Example. A starting rule for refresh: when cost per approved lead is above target at 2 checkpoints in a row and frequency has risen above about 3, launch new hooks on the same angle. The frequency figure is a rough guide that varies by geo, audience size and format.
steps.say: Here's how to spot creative fatigue. Example: a winning creative over seven days. Look at the two lines. Frequency climbs as the same people see it again, and cost per approved lead rises from about ten fifty to seventeen dollars. C T R falls too. That's fatigue. A starting rule: when cost per approved is above target at two checkpoints in a row, and frequency has risen above about three, launch new hooks on the same angle. Plan the refresh before you cross the kill line.

steps.h: Matching the lander to the angle
steps.p: When an angle wins, the lander should say the same thing as the ad. A lander built per angle keeps message match, which often lifts approval because buyers find what the ad promised.

d.why: Landvoo lets you build a lander variant per winning angle so the page repeats the ad's honest promise and approval holds up.

steps.say: When an angle wins, the lander should say the same thing as the ad. That's called message match, and it often lifts approval, because buyers find what the ad promised. The tool on screen, Landvoo, lets you build a lander variant per winning angle, so the page repeats the ad's honest promise and approval holds up.

steps.p: These testing mistakes give you wrong answers that look right. They waste the budget you spent on the test, which is the most expensive kind of waste.

a.title: Mistakes
items: Changing hooks inside a live test

b.title: Fixes
items: New hooks in a new ad

steps.say: These testing mistakes give you wrong answers that look right, which is the most expensive kind of waste. Compare the columns. No sub I D per ad, instead of the ad I D in a sub I D. Judging before leads are processed, instead of waiting. Changing hooks inside a live test, instead of putting new hooks in a new ad. And scaling twice in twenty four hours, instead of twenty percent steps, forty eight hours apart.

steps.h: New creatives need the same review
steps.p: Under pressure to refresh a fatigued winner, it is tempting to push new hooks live without review. Every new hook, cut and caption goes through the compliance checklist, however small the change.

d.text: Run every new creative and every edit through your claims file and visual checklist before launch.

steps.say: New creatives need the same review. Under pressure to refresh a fatigued winner, it's tempting to push new hooks live without checking them. But every new hook, cut and caption goes through the compliance checklist, however small the change. As the warning says, run every new creative and every edit through your claims file and visual checklist before launch.

steps.p: A steady routine keeps winners alive longer and replacements ready before fatigue hits. Use the same day each week, and use network sub-ID data rather than platform lead counts.
d: Pull approvals by sub-ID
Apply the rule card per ad set
Flag fatigue: rising CPA and frequency
Brief 3 to 5 new hooks for winning angles
Retire losers and log why
steps.say: Here's your weekly creative routine, on the same day each week, using network sub I D data rather than platform lead counts. Pull approvals by sub I D. Apply the rule card per ad set. Flag fatigue, where C P A and frequency are both rising. Brief three to five new hooks for winning angles. And retire losers, logging why. It keeps winners alive longer, and replacements ready before fatigue hits.

takeaways: Tag every ad with a sub-ID so approvals can be traced to creatives.
Apply the same kill, hold and scale rules per ad set using network-approved leads, after processing.
Watch for fatigue (rising cost per approved and frequency) and refresh with reviewed new hooks.
lessons.action: Set up sub-IDs on one offer link so the ad ID reaches the network, and write your creative rule card with the target, scale line, kill line and zero-approval spend for that offer.

glossary.def: A parameter on your affiliate link that the network records with each lead, used to trace leads to ads.
When results from a creative get worse because the same people have seen it too often.
Average number of times each person saw your ad.
When the lander repeats what the ad promised.

quiz.q: Why put the ad ID in a sub-ID?
options: So approvals can be traced to each creative
quiz.why: The network report then shows approvals per ad.

quiz.q: Target $15. Spent $54, 5 approved. Decision?
quiz.why: $54 ÷ 5 = $10.80, under the $12 scale line with 5 approved.

quiz.q: Target $15. Spent $24, 1 approved. Decision?
quiz.why: Spend is under 3 × target and there is 1 approved, so no kill rule applies yet.

quiz.q: Cost per approved rises for 2 checkpoints above target and frequency is about 3.5. What is likely?
options: Creative fatigue; launch new hooks on the angle
quiz.why: Rising cost with rising frequency is the classic fatigue pattern.

quiz.q: A new caption is added to a winning video. Does it need review?
options: Yes, every edit goes through the checklist
quiz.why: Small edits can add claims; everything is reviewed.

lessons.say_intro: In this final lesson you'll learn to test nutra creatives on money, not likes. You'll tag every ad so approvals trace back to it, apply kill, hold and scale rules per creative, and spot fatigue before it costs you.
lessons.say_outro: So, tag every ad with a sub I D, judge creatives on approved leads with the rule card, and refresh before fatigue crosses your kill line. Your task: set up sub I Ds on one offer link so the ad I D reaches the network, and write your creative rule card with the target, scale line, kill line and zero-approval spend for that offer. Now take the quiz.

exam.q: Which angle stays honest for a joint cream?
options: A cooling routine after a long day standing
exam.why: It describes a common situation and the product without diagnosis, shame or promise.

exam.q: A rival's cure-claim ad has run for 10 weeks. What do you do with it?
options: Take at most the lawful idea, never the claim or footage
exam.why: Long runners can still be illegal and copying footage infringes rights.

exam.q: Three hooks: A $12.50, B $11.00, C $19.00 per approved, target $15. C has the best CTR. Which to back?
exam.why: B has the best cost per approved lead; CTR alone misleads.

exam.q: Translated ad CPL $5, approval 35%. Localised CPL $6, approval 60%. Cost per approved?
A Kenyan native speaker translates 'soothing' to a word meaning 'heals'. What should catch this?
exam.why: Back-translation shows the meaning shifted into a medical claim.

exam.q: A creator was paid and given product. Their video has no disclosure. What do you do?
options: Add spoken or on-screen disclosure and use the platform's branded content tool
exam.why: Paid and gifted content must be disclosed.

exam.q: Target $15. Ad set spent $33, 0 approved after processing. Decision?
exam.why: Spend is over 2 × target with 0 approved.

exam.q: Target $15. Ad set spent $66, 6 approved. Decision?
You cannot tell which creative brought approved leads. What is missing?
options: A sub-ID with the ad ID on the link
exam.why: Without a sub-ID per ad, approvals cannot be traced to creatives.

exam.q: 8 creators at $70 each, 4 usable videos. Cost per usable video?
